explanations.18: This creates an associative array (like a dictionary/map) named AI_COMMANDS that can be accessed globally throughout the script — the 'g' flag makes it global, and 'A' makes it an associative array rather than a regular indexed array.
explanations.19: Same as line 18, but this array will store parameter type information for each command.
explanations.28: If the OLLAMA_HOST environment variable isn't set, it defaults to 'http://localhost:11434' — this lets users override where to find Ollama without changing the script.
explanations.39: Similar to line 28: if OLLAMA_MODEL isn't set, it defaults to 'qwen3-coder:30b', so the function can work out of the box without requiring environment setup.
explanations.49: The 'print -r --' is a safe way to output the prompt string without bash interpreting any special characters or escape sequences in it.
explanations.69: This checks if the text contains backticks (the triple-backtick code fence markers); the asterisks are wildcards that match any characters before or after.
explanations.75: The 'inside' variable acts as a toggle: each time we hit a line starting with backticks, we flip whether we're inside a fenced code block or not, then skip printing that fence line itself.
explanations.98: The ':A' after the variable name expands it to an absolute path — so if you pass a relative path like '../file.txt', it gets converted to the full path starting from the root.
explanations.99: This removes the current directory path from the beginning of the absolute path, leaving just the relative portion — if PWD is '/home/user/project' and path is '/home/user/project/src/file.txt', the result is 'src/file.txt'.
explanations.107: This line both tests and returns: it checks if the answer starts with 'y' or 'Y', and returns 0 (success) if true, 1 (failure) if false — this is how yes/no prompts return a success code.
explanations.126: It reads the AI_DIFF_MAX_CHARS environment variable if set, otherwise defaults to 12000 characters as the maximum diff size to send to the model.
explanations.143: The '(( ... ))' syntax evaluates a math expression; here it checks if the length of the diff is less than or equal to the max, and if so, returns the full diff.
explanations.154: This grep filters the diff to show only the structural lines (file headers and hunk markers starting with @@) while stripping out the actual line-by-line changes.
explanations.158: String slicing syntax: `${summary[1,$max]}` keeps only characters 1 through $max (inclusive), truncating everything after the character limit.
explanations.172: This line tries to find the 'bat' binary and stores its name in bat_bin, then constructs a preview command — if bat isn't found, preview stays as plain 'cat'.
explanations.173: The '&&' means 'if the previous command succeeded', so the preview command only gets updated if _ai_bat actually found bat; otherwise it falls back to cat.
explanations.238: The `${+AI_COMMANDS[$cmd]}` syntax checks whether the key $cmd exists in the AI_COMMANDS array — it returns true if the key is present, false otherwise.
explanations.250: The `${(ok)AI_COMMANDS}` syntax means 'give me the keys of AI_COMMANDS sorted alphabetically' — the 'o' flag sorts, and 'k' means keys rather than values.
explanations.269: This splits the parameter types string on spaces: if AI_PARAMS contains 'file language', this loop will iterate twice with param_type set to 'file', then 'language'.
